The Cambridge neighborhoods with the greatest rat issues

And how the city is getting smart to get rid of the rats

Rats are so ever present in the city of Cambridge that they have become a part of the city's cultural lexicon, appearing regularly in small talk, art exhibits, and, in neighboring Somerville, even titling the local musical festival: Ratchella.

These cultural appearances hint towards an ugly truth: rats are everywhere in the city. The Cambridge Day has reported on rats “dripping out of heaters” and construction in Riverside “unleashing [their] fury.” In 2020, Cambridge’s city manager declared what many residents already knew, “we’re still losing the battle” against rats.

Faced with this onslaught, the city has deployed new tactics, such as installing rat-proof Big Belly trash cans throughout the city and, as of 2023, deploying “Smart Box” rat traps, which electrically kill rats with a charge, and provide live kill totals. So, five years later, where does the battle stand? I analyzed Cambridge Commonwealth Connect, also known as 311, reports to see where the fighting was most intense—and if the city had made any progress.

The City of Cambridge encourages residents to report rodent sightings using 311 and makes all rodent reports available on their open data portal. After downloading the latest 311 data, I filtered to records that specifically mentioned rats in their description. In addition, since almost 80% of 311 rodent sightings with a description mention rats, I included general rodent reports that did not specifically mention another rodent (such as mice or raccoons), assuming that these reports were most likely about rats even if they didn’t mention them by name.

Rat-related 311 reports

Each dot represents a 311 rat report from 2016 to 2024

Rat reports are primarily concentrated in the eastern half of the city, with the highest concentrations in Central Square, the Port, and Cambridgeport.

To identify which neighborhoods have the highest concentrations of rat reports, I aggregated the data by census block. The darkest blocks, such as those on Broadway in East Cambridge, have the highest concentration of rat reports per square kilometer.

Since 2022, smart rat traps have been strategically deployed to rat hotspots across the city. The most productive trap, located in a pipe by 88 Allston St, has caught 614 rats since its installation in 2023.

So have these new rat strategies worked? Using the same 311 data, I calculated the number of rat reports per year since 2016. While rat reports ticked up between 2023 and 2024, overall they are down from a peak of 1,267 in 2021. As a percentage of total 311 requests, rat reports are down too, declining to 4.4% from a peak of 8.1% in 2021.

Further rat mitigation strategies may be coming soon. Cambridge and Somerville recently launched a rodent fertility control study in February, which uses Evolve, “a hormonal fertility control product designed to humanely curb rat reproduction.” With 420 rat reports already submitted in 2025, it’s clear that our struggle with rats is here to stay, but our new approaches appear to be working, and that should give us hope.
